records.value: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the East India Company’s administrative powers, possessions and armed forces to the British Crown. Responsibility in Britain passed to a Secretary of State for India, while the Crown appointed the viceroy and governors. Later constitutional reforms changed the institutions within this imperial framework. This arrangement is commonly described as the British Raj. It was an imperial system, rather than an independent national government. The mapped entity should not be read as proof of uniform direct British administration across all of the subcontinent. Princely states had a distinct position, and the geographical dataset’s authority fields provide only a simplified representation. This dossier keeps that distinction visible rather than treating administrative control as an unqualified statement of sovereignty.

records.value: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred the East India Company’s administrative powers, possessions and armed forces to the British Crown. Responsibility in Britain passed to a Secretary of State for India, while the Crown appointed the viceroy and governors. Later constitutional reforms changed the institutions within this imperial framework. This arrangement is commonly described as the British Raj. It was an imperial system, rather than an independent national government. The mapped entity should not be read as proof of uniform direct British administration across all of the subcontinent. Princely states had a distinct position, and the geographical dataset’s authority fields provide only a simplified representation. This dossier keeps that distinction visible rather than treating administrative control as an unqualified statement of sovereignty.

records.value: The source map labels this region Manchu Empire, although the Qing emperor had abdicated in February 1912. The Republic of China received full US diplomatic recognition in 1913. The republican government had not unified all of China under its control; the generalized 1914 outline should therefore be read as a schematic region rather than a verified boundary of central authority.

scope.description: The upstream Manchu Empire label is anachronistic after the 1912 abdication. records.value: Following his re-election in 1936, Franklin D. Roosevelt began a second presidential term on 20 January 1937, with John Nance Garner as vice-president. His first inauguration had taken place on 4 March 1933; the Twentieth Amendment changed the inauguration date for 1937 onward. Roosevelt communicated with the public through informal radio addresses. Early broadcasts discussed the banking crisis, the New Deal programme and economic recovery, followed by an address on public works and Social Security in 1935. His Good Neighbor Policy sought improved relations and trade with Latin America through a stated commitment to respect and non-intervention. The population figure shown separately is an earlier, geographically limited census observation, not a current-year estimate.

records.value: The United States entered the war in late 1941 and coordinated with Britain and the Soviet Union. Cooperation against Nazi Germany included disagreements over the second front. Roosevelt’s death in April 1945 brought Truman to the presidency.

Truman took office after Roosevelt’s death in April 1945. His presidential calendar documents the administration through January 1953. The end of the Second World War did not produce a new United States map identity: the presidency and bicameral Congress remained institutions of the same federal constitutional state. This profile covers the administration without attaching later presidents to earlier selected years.

records.value: After Hitler’s appointment as chancellor in January 1933, the Nazi leadership dismantled Germany’s democratic institutions and suppressed political opposition. The regime used emergency powers and legislation to concentrate authority, while excluding opponents from public life. Following President Hindenburg’s death in August 1934, Hitler combined presidential authority with the chancellorship. The Nazi Party dominated a dictatorship rather than a competitive parliamentary system. This overview describes the consolidated regime of the mid-1930s, without treating its later territorial conquests as facts about every selected year. The atlas’s boundary reconstructions are a separate geographical source and do not establish the constitutional or political status of every territory represented on the map.

records.value: The Meiji Constitution placed the emperor at the centre of the constitutional order. Its provisions described imperial sovereignty and provided for legislative power to be exercised with the Imperial Diet. The Diet consisted of a House of Peers and a House of Representatives. Ministers of state advised the emperor and bore responsibility for their advice. This dossier records those constitutional provisions rather than assuming that the formal document explains every aspect of political practice in the 1930s. Its curated coverage is limited to the imperial polity represented by the mapped identity. It does not use the post-war constitution or a modern government profile as a silent substitute for the selected historical period.

records.value: The war in China that expanded in 1937 increasingly shaped Japan’s foreign relations. Japanese military operations and territorial ambitions brought escalating tension with the United States, which opposed the expansion of the conflict. At home, the Meiji Constitution continued to define imperial sovereignty and a bicameral Imperial Diet. Prime ministers changed repeatedly in 1939 and 1940; the dated cabinet records preserve those transitions. Prefectural census figures describe a narrower territory than the whole empire.

records.value: The peace treaty took effect on 28 April 1952, ending the Allied occupation and restoring Japan to sovereign equality. The 1947 constitution continued to place sovereignty in the people, with an emperor who symbolised the state, a bicameral Diet and a cabinet responsible to it. This post-occupation setting differs both from the earlier imperial framework and from the first years of the new constitution under occupation. Changes of prime minister are recorded separately.

records.value: The Soviet Union was governed through a Communist Party dictatorship. By the mid-1930s, Joseph Stalin had eliminated major rivals and consolidated control over party and state. Forced collectivisation and centrally directed industrial development had imposed severe costs on the population. Political policing and repression were central instruments of government. During 1936–1938, public trials and mass persecution formed part of the Great Terror, which reached its height in 1937–1938. Leadership here refers to Stalin’s dominant position in the party-state system, rather than an assumed presidential or prime-ministerial office. The constitutional description and the practice of party dictatorship are kept distinct.

records.value: Churchill became prime minister in May 1940 and formed a wartime coalition. His Conservative affiliation should not be mistaken for the composition of that all-party administration. Britain’s war effort depended on military operations and cooperation with allies; the government continued to operate through parliamentary institutions. George VI remained monarch throughout the war. The leadership records preserve the change to Attlee in 1945 rather than assigning one prime minister to the entire transition year.

Attlee’s Labour government followed the 1945 election. Its programme expanded public services and nationalised important industries. The National Health Service and national insurance legislation were central to postwar reconstruction. Overseas, the government presided over independence for India and Pakistan and the end of British rule in other territories. These were changes in imperial relationships, not grounds for treating every formerly governed territory as a part of the United Kingdom’s domestic census population.
